{"docket_number": "9", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1966", "first_party": "United States", "first_party_label": "Appellant", "second_party": "Sealy, Inc.", "second_party_label": "Appellee", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Appeal", "lower_court": null, "argued": ["1967-04-20T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Did Sealy’s method of allocating territorial manufacturing licenses violate the Sherman Act?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Until about 1920, the Sealy Mattress Company was the sole manufacturer of Sealy products at its four factories in the Midwest and Southwest. By 1923, however, some 19 independent factories operated under Sealy licenses. Soon thereafter, these licensees and new owner E. E. Edwards formed the Sealy Corporation. Sealy continued to license the use of the Sealy mark to independent stock-holding bedding manufacturers.

In 1925, the licensees agreed on a system of allocating exclusive territories to market Sealy products. Each manufacturer had an exclusive territory in his license contract; this contract prohibited each manufacturer from selling outside of that territory. Around this time, the licensee-stockholders and Sealy began collaborating to fix and police the minimum and maximum prices charged by retailers of Sealy products, the advertised prices of Sealy products, and the means of inducing retailers to adhere to these prices. In 1933, Sealy Corporation reorganized into Sealy, Incorporated. Sealy, Inc. made a new provision that any new manufacturers coming into the organization must purchase Sealy stock. In the 1940’s, Sealy’s business increased and many new licensees joined to cover previously open territories.

The Sherman Act provided that every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce was illegal. The United States brought a civil action against Sealy, Inc. charging that it violated the Sherman Act by setting minimum retail prices and by forcing retailers to adhere to those prices. It also alleged that Sealy, Inc.’s exclusive territorial arrangements violated the Sherman Act. The district court held that Sealy, Inc.’s price fixing violated the Sherman Act, but that its territorial arrangements did not. The United States appealed the district court’s ruling on the legality of Sealy, Inc.’s licensing structure.

", "conclusion": "

Yes. In a 6-1 decision written by Justice Abraham Fortas, the Court held that Sealy’s licensing structure was a horizontal restraint of trade, a per se violation of the Sherman Act. He noted that the licensees controlled the day-to-day business of Sealy through the board of directors and the executive committee, including the grant, assignment, reassignment, and termination of exclusive territorial licenses. Justice Fortas held that Sealy’s behavior was an aggregation of trade restraints, reasoning that Sealy’s territorial restraints were a part of its admittedly unlawful price fixing scheme. While acknowledging that the territorial limitations served other purposes, he reasoned that their connection to price fixing was enough to require they be condemned as an unlawful restraint of trade.

Justice John Harlan dissented. He argued that Sealy’s territorial licensing structure was a vertical arrangement not prohibited by the Sherman Act. He described the main purpose of Sealy’s licensing structure as the proper exploitation of the Sealy name and trademarks by licensed bedding manufacturers. Justice Harlan argued that the territorial restrictions were secondary or ancillary to that purpose. He rejected the majority’s theory that Sealy’s actions were an aggregation of trade restraints, noting that the district court did not address the reasonableness of Sealy’s territorial arrangements.

Justices Tom Clark and Byron White took no part in the decision of the case.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "The United States Appellant v. Seeley, Inc. Mr. Friedman. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. The appellee, Seeley, Inc. holds various trademarks on bedding products. Seeley itself does no manufacturing, but it in turn licenses about 30 independent firms who do make bedding under the Seeley name in return for royalties which they pay to Seeley. In addition to licensing the trademarks, Seeley performs various other functions such as ensuring quality control of the products, research and development, and national advertising. The licensees to whom Seeley gives the right to use the trademark in turn collectively own about 90% of the stock of Seeley and elect all of the directors. The question in this civil antitrust case, which is here on direct appeal to the District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, is whether the provisions in the Seeley licensing contracts, which prohibit the licensees directly or indirectly from selling any of the Seeley trademark products outside of the particular area for which they are licensed, constitutes a restraint of trade which is unreasonable per se under Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The Seeley Company is a descendant of a firm known as Sugar Land Industries, which for many years had been itself manufacturing bedding under the Seeley trademark, and then beginning in the 1920s started licensing independent firms to manufacture bedding. In 1923, Sugar Land Industries decided to go out of the bedding business. And what it did was, it in turn sold all of its rights under the trademarks to a man named Edwards, who in effect acted as a promoter. And Edwards and the then 19 firms that were the licensees of Sugar Land Industries organized the predecessor of the Seeley Company. And the Seeley Company then in turn gave licenses to all of these 19 firms. The Seeley Company expanded thereafter. More licensees were taken in. During the Depression, the number of its licensees dropped to eight. And in 1933, the previous Seeley was reorganized into the present Apelle, which has continued in business substantially in that form since that time. Under the bylaws of Seeley, all the directors of the firm must be either licensees themselves or representatives of licensees. As I have indicated collectively, the licensees hold 90% or more of the stock, although not in any particular proportion either to their business or their interests. And there's also a provision in the bylaws that no licensee shall hold any more than 25% of the stock. Now, since the origin of the Seeley Company, there have been these territorial restrictions in its licensees. As far back as 1925, when the predecessor to the present Seeley was in the process of organization, a motion was adopted at a convention of all the Seeley licensees, which recommended the territories be permanently fixed. Now, I would like to just read briefly to the court a typical one of these license provisions limiting the territories. This one is taken from a 1948 contract, but they are substantially identical. And it's set forth to page 1182 of the record. After first... After first... This is in volume four, Mr. Justice. The contract first assigns... At pages 1176 to 1177, the specific territory covered by the license. And you'll see it's quite specific. It gives it in terms of states and is then broken down into counties. And then the particular provision, which is subparagraph 4-4b, says that the licensee shall not sell or deliver any Seeley products outside of licensee's exclusive territory, nor sell nor deliver Seeley products if licensee knows or has reason to believe that the purchaser intends to resell or deliver the same for resale out of licensee's exclusive territory. In other words, what this means is that a Seeley licensee cannot directly sell outside of its territory, and furthermore, it cannot sell to a customer if it knows or has reason to believe that the customer in turn is going to reship it into someone else's territory for resale. Do these 30 licenses cover the entire country? Virtually. They do. They're broken up on a geographical basis, and as far as I know, the company does operate throughout the country. And does that number 30 change from time to time? Well, it has. It has. It has. They carve out other ones. It has changed, Mr. Chief Justice, in two ways. For example, there have been instances when Seeley has not been satisfied with the way a particular licensee has been operating, and they have hired someone else, giving them the franchise. And also, over the past, as I shall come to in a moment, there have been situations where Seeley felt that a particular licensee was not properly exploiting its territory, and they broke it down and would put in a new licensee. For example, if you had a licensee in New Jersey and another one in Virginia, they might decide that neither of those was adequately serving Maryland, and they would, in effect, give the Maryland territory to. The licensee, if I may, authors suggest, the number is not fixed. 30 is not a fixed number. It could be 35 next year. It could be 25 next year. Is it claimed that in the origin of this matter, the formation of Seeley, that this was simply a front for a horizontal and territorial? No. No, we do not sell claim. We did allege that in the district court. We did allege in the district court that Seeley was just a subterfuge or a front for an illegal scheme to divide markets. We are not urging that in this court. We can see that... That was found against you. We're not challenging that. We can see that Seeley does perform perfectly proper functions. We do not say it's a cover. We do not say there was anything illegal in the organization. But we do say, as I shall develop, that the nature of this restraint is such that it basically is the result of the product of competitors, and therefore, for reasons which I will develop, we think it is within the per se rule. Now, these licensees are stockholders? The licensees are all stockholders at the present time. They're not required to be under the organization of Seeley, but, in fact, they are. And the only people who are stockholders other than licensees are one or two former officers of the company. I think the president is. Would it be, in your view, a violation of antitrust law for these 30 manufacturers to own substantially all the stock of Seeley? Well, not the mere act of owning it, no, Mr. Justice. We think what we're attacking is the provision and the licenses under which each one is kept in his own territory. We don't challenge the basic concept of a joint venture by which these 30 licensees, you have this Seeley organization, as a means of really using the trademark that has been developed. We don't challenge. Well, I suppose that if you start with the assumption that there is a valid joint venture, you wouldn't expect the joint ventures to compete with each other anyway, then. Well, we think, Mr. Justice, it's a joint venture only insofar as the use of the trademark is concerned. We would think that as independent firms, as independent manufacturers of betting... But they're not independent if they're stockholders. I mean, they're... Well, they're independent in the sense that they're not controlled by Seeley, and they're also independent in the sense that each one makes his own judgments as how best to exploit his particular market. Now, in addition... So do you or do you not submit to us that this should be treated as if it were a horizontal conspiracy? Yes, we do, Mr. Justice. We do think that basically this is the same as it can properly be treated as the... Well, the same rule should apply to this situation as should apply if you had an ordinary horizontal division of markets. That's not the answer. Do you or do you not say to us that this is, in substance and in actual operation, a horizontal conspiracy? Maybe I can get at it that way. Well, we do say that. Yes, Mr. Justice. Now, I don't see how you can say that and at the same time make the responses that you did to Mr. Justice Douglas's questions. Because, Mr. Justice, the conspiracy we say, the horizontal conspiracy we say, is the agreement to divide the territory. The agreement that no one of these licensees will compete with any other of the licensees in the sale of this property. Well, that's not an agreement among the distributors. Because that's an agreement in form, in a way, between Sealy and each distributor. Now, if you're saying that this is a horizontal conspiracy, don't you have to say that we have to treat Sealy as an instrumentality of the distributors, a device, in effect, that they've used for the purpose of making this agreement? Well, Mr. Justice, let me answer it this way. We say it is an instrumentality in the sense that this is the method through which these market divisions are made. We don't say it's a cover for this, but we do say it's a cover for this, and we say that basically, that basically, the end result of this, the effect of this on competition is the same as though you had the Sealy... You had no territorial restraints in the licenses themselves. Each man was just given a territory, and there's nothing said about going beyond the territory. And then they all got together and said, well, let's not compete too hard, let's divide it up. We think in terms of the practical effect, it's the same. You're saying it's not that we ought to think about it as something naughty. We ought to think about it as a cover, but think about it as a device. Is that the distinction that you want us to make? No, I think, Mr. Justice, we're urging that you look at it to see what, in effect, it does, what its effect on competition is, and what its source is, how this particular thing works, what are the factors that led the parties to inaugurate it. Well, to do that, in light of the case of this court, decisions of this court, as I understand it, it's quite important whether we start with the proposition that this is a horizontal or a vertical dispute. Well, I think, Mr. Justice, it has some elements of both, perhaps. It has some elements of both. In form, at least, it seems to be vertical. But what we're suggesting is that even though in form, it's vertical, it's a practical effect. It's a practical effect. It should be treated as the same as though it were a direct horizontal agreement among the parties. Now, let me add one other thing, if I may, just to come back to the facts for a moment, that there is a penalty under the licenses for every mattress product that is sold outside of the area. There's a penalty of $10 for every mattress that is shipped outside of the territory. And this is collected by Sealy and then remitted to the territories that have been invaded. Now, it is true, as our opponents stress, that under these licenses, Sealy licensees are free to sell non-trademarked bedding outside of their exclusive areas. The restriction only applies to products sold under the Sealy licensee. But the record shows that the amount of such non-Sealy products is relatively small. For the last three years shown by the record, 1957 to 1959, the total sales by all licensees of Sealy brand products range from $52 to $54 million. The total sales by these same licensees of their own private brand products range from just under $3 million to $2.5 million, or roughly only 2.5 percent. I'm sorry, 5 percent of the total sales. Now, as might be... Are there any price maintenance features in connection to these licenses? Yes, Mr. Justice, I was going to come to that. Another element, I'll just say this, another element of our complaint, charged that Sealy had engaged in retail price fixing. The district court found in our favor on that charge, entered an injunction, and Sealy has not appealed from that phase of the case. So that the only issue before this court is the legality of the territorial restraints. Now, it's not surprising in view of these detailed provisions over territories that there were frequent disputes among the licensees. There were constant disputes over whether a particular city, a particular county, sometimes even a particular customer, was in the territory of one or the other. In addition, there were disputes arising out of the claim that a licensee sold in one territory to a customer who in turn shipped to another. For example, in the mid-1950s, there was a controversy for several years between the Chicago licensee and the Louisville licensee. Over the fact that the Chicago man was selling to a store in his territory, and this store in turn had branches in the Memphis, I'm sorry, in the Louisville territory, and therefore the customer was shipping over to the Louisville territory, and the Louisville people objected to that on the ground. The Chicago man could not directly or indirectly sell into the Louisville territory. Now, when these disputes were brought to the attention of the Sealy officials, as they very frequently were, Sealy people recognized they had no power to solve these disputes. They couldn't force them, one of the parties, to give up territory, and they therefore generally suggested to the parties that the appropriate solution would be for them to try to voluntarily work the dispute out. A couple of examples of this. In 1953, the Sealy official recognized that the Louisville licensee should properly have certain territory adjacent to him that was actually the territory of Memphis, because, as he described it, the Louisville licensee could service these counties much better than the Memphis plant can, as he is considerably closer. But he then went on to say there was nothing he could do about it unless the Memphis licensee would be agreeable to giving the counties up. Then a rather dramatic and colorful example took place in 1956, which is 683 of the record in Volume 3. The Louisville licensee had again, this time had requested Sealy, that it should be given some territory. And the Sealy president replied as follows. He said that, unfortunately, all territories are under contract, which requires voluntary acquiescence to any suggestions of relignment. This writer, over a period of years, has found this to be a most difficult problem. It can be compared to the child who has three large lollipops, the size of which is such that she cannot put more than one in her mouth, and therefore the two other virtually are of no particular value to her. But you know how kids are trying to get them to give up anything that they have. The similarity might sound strange, but that is exactly the same position I find myself in when I ask any Sealy licensee to relinquish a little piece of territory, regardless of how miserable a job they may be doing in it. Now, the record shows that there have been instances where these territorial limitations have had an adverse effect on the business, the overall business of Sealy. This example is something happened in 1955. There was a chain of stores in the New York City area known as the Darling Stores. There are, I believe, 42 stores. Twenty of them were located in the New York City area of the state of New York. The other 22 were located in Connecticut and New Jersey. The main office of the store was in New York, and the licensee who had the New York territory made contact with the firm and was able to sell them the Sealy line. They were interested in it. But they said that they didn't want to buy the whole chain except through one source. And the Connecticut and New Jersey licensees refused to permit the New York licensee to sell to the Darling Stores for those particular stores that were in their areas and not in the New York licensee's area. And the result of this, as the New York licensee complained in a letter, was he said he just lost this account. And not only he, but obviously the whole Sealy operation lost the account. That is set forth at page 859 of the record. Then another example was something stated in 1953 by a Chicago, the Chicago licensee. He had a customer with four stores, some of them in his territory and some of them in the Memphis licensee's territory. And the customer indicated he would like to buy for the four stores and would like to buy from the Chicago man. But the Chicago man couldn't do this. As he explained, and this is at record 647, he said that under the existing Sealy setup, this is simply a dream. Of course, it is not understandable to the dealer, and the only ultimate loser is Sealy. And in that same year, the president of Sealy, that's 1953, stated at the director's meeting that he felt the exclusive territory provision would ultimately hinder the national growth of Sealy. And in the following discussion at the board meeting, nearly every member of the board stated that this contract provision caused his plant real and serious difficulties. Now, I'd like to just refer to one point which the appellee stresses in connection with this territory, these adverse impacts on the territory. Sealy points out quite correctly that there were a number of instances in which licensees voluntarily gave up territory they were not adequately serving to Sealy to enable Sealy either to reassign it to another licensee or sometimes to combine it with other territories to put in a brand new licensee in the area. And they suggest the fact that the individual licensees were willing to give up territory to Sealy indicates that, in fact, Sealy was something separate and distinct. The interests it represented were different from those of the licensees. We think that this situation merely reflects the following facts of life in the mattress industry. The basic success of the Sealy sales program depended primarily on the effectiveness and extent of its national advertising. That was the basic reason the whole program was set up, to enable Sealy small mattress makers to advertise on a national basis. And it seems reasonable that when a businessman, a licensee, gives up some territory that he is not adequately serving, all that this reflects is a value judgment on his part that, in the long run, he will be better off having this territory adequately exploited. That is, if the territory is adequately exploited, it will produce more revenues. These more revenues will go to Sealy and part through the royalties which they pay, which are based on a volume. Sealy, in turn, will have additional money with which to spend for national advertising. And the national advertising will redound, ultimately, to the betterment of the licensee, so that he will be better off in the territory that he is vigorously exploiting with the aid of this more substantial advertising program. Now, as I have indicated to Mr. Justice Harlan, the complaint in this case charged both that these territorial restraints were illegal and that there was price fixing. At the close of the government's case, Sealy moved to dismiss the complaint. The district court denied that motion, but stated at page 13 of the record that, let me say, the court says, however, let me say that should there ever be a decree, there will be nothing in it finding that the territorialization, in my opinion, is a violation of the antitrust laws. That phase of the case. As a result of this, Sealy limited the presentation of its evidence to the price fixing phase of the case. And after Sealy had rested on this phase of the case, the government, in colloquies at record 45 and 46, strongly urged Sealy to put in any defense it would have on the territorialization. There are repeated instances of this. At page 45, Mr. Jenkinson says, I want him to put his defense in. And then at the top of page 46, Mr. Jenkinson, the chief government's trial counsel, says, all I can say is that I am urging you to put in any defense you have on territorialization in this record. And the court continued, I think the record clearly shows that you have urged him on everything but your bended knee to put in more evidence. Now, the district court, in disposing of the case, wrote no opinion. Did the court take the position in the district court that this was illegal per se? The price fixing? No, no, the territorialization. The government did, yes. It did? The government did, made it explicitly. Well, of course, if that's correct, there is no defense. That is correct, Mr. Justice. There's no point in anybody putting in it, trying to put in it. There's no point. But on the other hand, Mr. Justice, I suppose in determining whether the validity of these territorial restrictions are to be considered per se, it is important to analyze the problem in terms, as I shall do in a few minutes, first, what the impact of these restraints are on competition, and secondly, whether this is the kind of restraint as to which there is any reasonable likelihood that it could be justified. And I make this point because of the claim of our opponents that it's unfair for us now to be switching theory a little bit and to be urging to going into the substantive merits of these things, whereas they just, as they say, there's no record on this. Well, I do suggest that the record could have been developed on this, and it didn't. As I say, I think I can, I hope to demonstrate to the court that nothing they could put in would justify these restraints. Now, the... Well, is it your theory, Mr. Freeman, that if the court does not agree with you that this is a per se violation, that the case should be remanded, or do you think that that puts an end to the case? Well, I... Why not ask... Suppose we make a rivalry conclusion somewhat like that in White Motor. Is the government asking us to remand the case, or do you say that if we find that, if we conclude that it's not a per se violation, that the district court should be affirmed? Now, we're not asking for remand in this case, Mr. Justice. This is unlike White Motors, where we have gotten summary judgment in our favor, and it had to be. We present the case to this court on the per se theory, and I would assume it's... So if we disagree with you on per se, that ends... I would think so, Mr. Justice. Now, as I said, the court wrote no opinion, but rendered very detailed findings, and the theory on which the court held against us on our per se claim, I think, is set... can be spelled out from the findings. I'd just like to summarize them rather briefly. First, the court found that there was no conspiratorial purpose among Seeley to divide the United States into territories. The court found that the proper... The main purpose of this restriction was the proper exploitation of the Seeley name and trademarks by the licensees, that Seeley had imposed these territorial restraints as a necessary ancillary restraint to the main purpose. The court went on to find that it was obvious that an essential inducement to the prospective licensees to get them to take the obligations of a licensee with these territorial restraints, and finally, a conclusory finding that Seeley's activities, and I quote, have been directed not toward market division among licensees, but toward obtaining additional licensees and more intensive sales coverage. Now, we start with the basic theory, the basic doctrine on which per se rules in the antitrust field rest. I think, as this court has indicated, they reflect a recognition that there are certain kinds of restraints on competition, kinds of restraints, types of restraints, whose purpose and effect ordinarily are so clearly anti-competitive, and the possible justifications for which are ordinarily so tenuous as to make it appropriate in the interest of effective antitrust enforcement to condemn all restraints of this character without the need for an extended investigation into either the impact of the restraint in the particular case or the possible justifications in pro-competitive terms of the restraint in the particular case. You mean without any investigation. Without any investigation, yes. As distinguished, I'm suggesting Mr. Justice Harlan, as distinguished in the ordinary reasonableness case where you examine the impact of the particular restraint in the particular industry. I would just comment on your qualification extended investigation. Without any investigation. Because ordinarily, unfortunately, as will appear from the next case with the 22-volume record in a reasonableness case, the investigation tends to be very extensive. Now, our submission to the court is that this particular restraint comes within that category and is therefore appropriate to treat it as per se. And I'd like to discuss, make the argument in two branches. First, the effect of this on competition, and secondly, possible justifications that have been suggested for it. Now, the first, it seems to me, and the very obvious fact, which cannot be denied, is that this restraint completely and directly eliminates all competition in Sealy brand products between the manufacturers of those products. Even though a particular manufacturer might be better able to serve a particular market, even though refusing to permit a particular manufacturer to serve a particular outlet which has branches in another territory may result in losing the entire account for Sealy, as was true in the example of the Darling Stores case I gave a few moments ago, nevertheless, under this restraint, you cannot do that. And also the direct effect of this, of course, is to deny the retail outlets of Sealy products the benefits of any competition among the manufacturers, price competition or any other competition, when they purchase their Sealy products for resale. And we think that this intra-brand competition, the competition among Sealy products, is just as much entitled to the protection of the antitrust laws as the traditional inter-brand competition. Indeed, the rule prohibiting resale price maintenance, we think necessarily must rest upon that premise, because what resale price maintenance is, is eliminating price competition among sellers of the same product. Well, I assume you're going on to add some factual elements here, because Sealy is a trademark product, isn't it? Yes. And would you agree that there would be no reason, no legal reason at all, why Sealy could not permit designated manufacturers to use its trademark? That's clearly correct. And deny the use of that trademark to other manufacturers. Yes. Now, how do you take this case out of that generality? What are the factors here that you urge as taking the case out of that general rule? Well, Mr. Justice, we don't question the right of Sealy to license these people. We do question, we do challenge the right of Sealy, which in effect is controlled by the licensees, to limit the particular territory in which each licensee may sell. That's what we challenge. We think this licensing arrangement, this program, can be operated just as effectively without these restraints, these particular restraints. And that's what I would like to develop. What you're really challenging now is the theory of exclusive distributorship of trademark products. Because an exclusive distributorship, by definition, I think, means that there is a territorial limitation. We are challenging, if I may qualify it in one respect, Mr. Justice, we are challenging the system of exclusive territories by, in trademark distribution, where the trademark license score is itself owned by the licensee. All right. Now what you're doing, then, is basing your keys on the existence of horizontal agreements for the limitation of territory. That is correct. Now, I'd like to just briefly explain why we think, why we think the fact that it is horizontal is significant in terms of the basic justifications of the per se rule, in terms of the likelihood that this is the kind of restraint that can be justified. We're not arguing the case just pinning labels that's horizontal and that's the end of it. We think there are very strong policy reasons, strong economic reasons to justify this result. Ordinarily, when you have an independent manufacturer who is licensing other, authorizing other people to sell his products, his major interest is to try to produce the most vigorous competition among his dealers. In other words, he's interested in selling as much of the product as he can to induce these people to compete more vigorously. And therefore, when you have a situation in which the manufacturer himself takes the initiative in limiting competition among his distributors, it seems a reasonable inference that this limitation, at least in his mind, is designed to accomplish some purpose serving primarily his best interest. In other words, and I think this is the basic rationale of the White Motor case, there's enough of a reasonable probability or possibility that in the long run, the manufacturer may properly have concluded that his product overall can be most effectively promoted, that is, interbrand competition between his product and the other product, can be most effectively pushed by having these limitations on his licensees. And therefore, we think it's appropriate in that situation where the initiative comes from above or it goes down, it's appropriate in that situation to at least look and consider what the justifications are. Why aren't you foreclosed from that argument by the findings of fact and by your statement at the beginning of the argument that you don't claim that there was any horizontal arrangement in the origins of this that tainted the original Seeley setup? You're arguing as sort of a horizontal matter of law conspiracy. Well, we're arguing, I suppose, that's so interesting. Let me say, I'd just like to come back to one thing. I said that we didn't think horizontally at the original setup that this was imposed, that this thing was imposed, that this whole licensing scheme was utilized as a cover, as a cover for the division of markets. But we do have, which I mentioned earlier, at the very outset, the first meeting of this early convention, they did agree to fix the territorial boundaries at an early convention in 1925. And in addition to that, we do have the whole pattern of the operation of Seeley, that Seeley operates in a way that basically it is responsive to the interests of its stockholders. So Seeley really has no function, separate and apart, from the interests of its stockholders. That's what it's there for, to further the interests of the licensees.
